subject: chemistry
title: Distillation
welcome_lead: Boil it, catch the vapour, cool it back: pure liquid out of a salty mess.
meta_desc: Discover distillation in this KS3 chemistry adventure on separating liquids from solutions and mixtures.
final_note: You can now extract pure water from sea water using distillation.

walkthroughs.body_html:
To separate water from a salt solution:

1) Heat the solution. Water boils at 100°C; salt does not.
2) Water vapour rises into the condenser.
3) Cold water around the condenser cools the vapour, turning it back to pure water.

Fractional distillation separates a mixture of liquids. The liquid with the lowest boiling point evaporates first and is collected first.

Used to separate crude oil!
Distillation makes fresh water from sea water in dry countries, separates alcohol from water, and turns crude oil into petrol, diesel and other useful fuels.

mcqs.q: Why can an endothermic reaction still be spontaneous?
options: Benzene cannot react at all because it's too stable.
Endothermic reactions are never spontaneous because they require energy input.
All endothermic reactions are spontaneous at room temperature.
If the entropy increase (TΔS) is large enough to outweigh the positive ΔH, ΔG can still be negative.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition reactions?
options: Adding across a C=C would destroy the stable delocalised pi system; substitution preserves the aromatic ring.
All endothermic reactions are spontaneous at room temperature.
Benzene cannot react at all because it's too stable.
Benzene contains three normal alternating double bonds and behaves like an alkene with three C=C.

options: The order of reaction is always equal to the number of reactants in the equation.
The order of reaction with respect to each reactant equals its coefficient in the balanced equation.
No — orders must be determined experimentally; they often differ from the stoichiometric coefficients.
All endothermic reactions are spontaneous at room temperature.
